briefs.headline: Industrial output grows 6.7% on manufacturing, electricity
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Industrial production grew 6.7% in Sept as against 6.1% expansion recorded a year ago, on account of strong manufacturing and electricity output.
Sequentially, however, industrial production witnessed deceleration from a downward revised figure of 7.8% in Aug, official data released Wednesday showed. During April-Sept, the index of industrial production (IIP) grew 6.8%, compared with 4.4% a year ago.
Manufacturing, which has a weight of 76% in the index, grew 7.6% as 17 out of 23 industry groups witnessed an increase in output, led by beverages, electrical equipment, transport equipment, rubber, textiles, furniture among others.
Electricity and gas supply expanded 11.2% on account of higher temperature due to heat wave conditions. Electricity production from conventional sources recorded double-digit growth (16.5%) in Sept, while there was a moderate growth in electricity output from renewable sources (4.3%). The newly added water supply, sewerage and waste management sector grew 5.8%. Activity in the mining and quarrying contracted further (-6.2%) during the month, led by the non-metallic minerals segment with output declining in eight of the last nine months.
In the use-based category -- capital goods (10.4%) and intermediate goods (12.2%) industries registered double-digit output, reflecting the impact of sustained public capex in the economy. Capital goods, too, grew 7.2% during the month.
Output in consumer durables, which reflect consumer sentiments, witnessed deceleration (6%) during the month, while consumer non-durables recorded acceleration in growth (1.4%) in Sept, after remaining in the contractionary zone in Aug.

briefs.headline: 3 Wall Street firms agree to pay up to $100,000 a month to get Trump’s posts faster
briefs.deck: Donald Trump's Truth API, a subscription-based social media service, is attracting a diverse clientele, including Bloomberg and various trading firms, by offering rapid access to his posts. This service's growing popularity raises ethical questions about the commercialization of presidential communication and its potential effects on market dynamics. Amid ongoing legal challenges and mounting…
briefs.bodyText:
US President Donald Trump’s paid social media service, Truth API, has found customers, with Bloomberg and two high-frequency trading firms paying for faster access to his posts. The service costs financial institutions up to $100,000 a month.
Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter, cited by Reuters, said Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading, both of which specialise in algorithmic and automated trading strategies, have also signed up for the service.
The deals give subscribers a timing advantage over people who monitor Trump’s posts on the app themselves.
The arrangement has raised concerns about the sale of faster access to statements by a sitting president, particularly because his posts can influence financial markets.
It also comes as Trump Media and Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social, faces legal challenges over the paid service and questions about the potential use of presidential communications for commercial gain.
How Truth API works
Trump Media and Technology Group announced the faster-access product in July, pitching it to trading firms and other financial institutions. The service is designed to deliver Trump’s posts more quickly than a person could obtain them by repeatedly checking Truth Social.
Trump Media officials have put the timing advantage at 50 milliseconds. For financial firms using automated trading systems, that difference can matter when a presidential statement triggers a change in asset prices.
High-frequency traders rely on software to scan news headlines, company announcements and government statements for information that could move markets. Their systems can read and analyse the information before executing trades in thousandths of a second.
The potential consequences of Trump’s social media posts were evident in April, when oil futures fell after he announced a ceasefire in the Iran war on Truth Social.
An application programming interface, or API, acts as a digital bridge that allows one computer system to communicate with another. In this case, the product gives subscribers faster access to the president’s posts, which they can use in their trading or financial information systems.
Who is paying for the service?
According to a Reuters report, Bloomberg, Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading are among the organisations that have signed up for Truth API.
In August, Trump Media told investors it had "signed more than 10 customer agreements”. Reuters was unable to independently confirm that figure.
The company did not identify its customers but said they were primarily Wall Street trading firms paying between $60,000 and $100,000 a month. The latest deals indicate that the product has attracted both financial trading firms and a news and data provider.
Reuters, which competes with Bloomberg in financial news, said in a statement: "We will assess the service, but have no current plans to subscribe."
Trump Media defended the product in a statement, saying: “Truth Social offers an industry-standard API product for which there is significant demand across industries. We take customer confidentiality seriously. This reporting is based on misleading information being peddled by anonymous sources aimed at harming our company, customers and shareholders.”
The company has not publicly named the subscribers in its August investor update, and the three firms named in the report declined to comment.
Why the paid feed has drawn criticism
The paid service has drawn criticism for giving subscribers faster access to a president’s statements, potentially offering financial firms an advantage when his posts move markets. The deals are likely the first time a business linked to a sitting president has sold access to his statements.
In July, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Adam Schiff of California asked the US Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether the service violated securities laws. They called it a “shocking abuse” of office by a president seeking personal gain.
A Trump Media and Technology Group spokesperson said, “Congressional Democrats continue to mischaracterize Truth API either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information.”
In August, Intercept Media and the non-profit Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump, seeking to stop the White House from posting official government announcements exclusively on Truth Social. The ongoing lawsuit describes the service as "profoundly corrupt" and alleges violations of the First and Fifth Amendments.
Trump Media’s financial portfolio
The commercial arrangement has also drawn attention to the ownership of Trump Media. The president’s family trust owns 41% of the company, and Trump is the trust’s sole beneficiary.
The Truth API deals come as Trump Media faces a steep decline in its stock market value.
Shares of the company have fallen more than 50% so far this year. Its market value has also been volatile since it went public in March 2024.
The company closed at a market value of about $8 billion on its debut in March 2024, but is now worth about $1.8 billion.
Since 2024, Trump Media has lost about $1.76 billion, including non-cash charges.

briefs.headline: India, Mexico begin talks for trade pact
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India and Mexico have signed the terms of reference marking the formal commencement of negotiations for a preferential trade agreement.
“The negotiations will focus on identifying mutually beneficial opportunities to expand trade, facilitate investment and strengthen supply chain linkages. Leveraging the complementarities between the two economies will be important in deepening commercial ties and fostering greater cooperation across key sectors,” commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal said in a social media post.
The initiative follows the understanding reached between PM Shri Narendra Modi and President Claudia Sheinbaum during their meeting on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Canada in June 2025, an official statement said.
Having the agreement is critical for Indian exporters as Mexico increased import duty from about 5% to as high as 50% on over 1,400 products from countries that do not have free trade agreements, including India, China, South Korea, Thailand and Indonesia. India’s exports to the Mexico added up to $5.7 billion during the last financial year with automobiles and auto parts adding up to close to $1.5 billion.

briefs.headline: Adani explores buyout of Dutch energy co VTTI
briefs.bodyText:
Billionaire 
Gautam Adani
, India’s richest person, is exploring a potential acquisition of Dutch energy storage group VTTI as supply disruptions make the facilities more valuable for energy trading, people familiar with the matter said.
Adani Group
, the tycoon’s power-to-ports conglomerate, is among suitors that have been evaluating Rotterdam-based VTTI, according to the people. A deal could value the company at around $3.4 billion, they said.
Australian infrastructure manager IFM Investors Pty and energy and commodities group Vitol SA each own around 45% of VTTI, while Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. holds the remaining 10%. Adnoc is considering selling out of VTTI completely and the other co-owners may also look to reduce their positions in the company in any deal, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing confidential information.
Deliberations are ongoing and there’s no certainty they’ll result in a transaction, the people said. Other bidders have also been pursuing a stake in VTTI, they said. A representative for Adani Group didn’t immediately respond to queries. Spokespeople for IFM, Adnoc and VTTI declined to comment. A representative for Vitol didn’t immediately comment.
VTTI operates terminals used to store fuels and chemicals, including fossil fuels, biofuels and solvents. 
The company has a global presence. Adani Group’s portfolio houses infrastructure assets including airports, roads and data centers, as well as mining and defense assets. Its founder is India’s wealthiest person with an estimated net worth of about $105.7 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
Listed flagship Adani Enterprises in July raised Rs 15,000 crore ($1.6 billion) from institutional investors to help fund capital expenditures and possible debt repayment. The following month, Gautam Adani won dismissal of US securities fraud charges — a victory in a blockbuster case that had threatened his conglomerate’s expansion. Adani Group has been looking at acquisitions overseas to help accelerate growth. It recently explored the acquisition of a stake in Associated British Ports, the UK’s largest port operator, people with knowledge of the matter have said.

stories.headline: Josh Inglis, Alex Carey put Australia in control of third Test against SA
stories.deck: Australia took a lead over South Africa in the third Test after Day 2. Josh Inglis and Alex Carey formed a significant fifth-wicket partnership, with Inglis scoring 85 not out. Earlier, Matt Renshaw contributed with 74 runs while Cameron Green added 65 runs to strengthen Australia's innings. The match saw South Africa taking critical wickets before Inglis and Carey stabilized the innings.
stories.bodyText:
Josh Inglis
 and 
Alex Carey
 stitched together an unbeaten fifth-wicket partnership of 145 runs to put Australia in command of the deciding third Test against South Africa, taking the visitors to 330/4 at stumps on Day 2.
Inglis remained unbeaten on 85 off with nine fours and two sixes, while Carey scored 51 not out as Australia edged past South Africa’s first-innings total of 329 in the final over of the day.
Playing his first Test since December, Inglis led Australia's recovery in a dominant final session, during which the visitors added 139 runs without losing a wicket. Carey, meanwhile, registered his first half-century in 12 Test innings. The pair also recorded Australia's first century-plus fifth-wicket stand against South Africa since 2014.
Earlier, 
Matt Renshaw
 scored 74 and Cameron Green contributed 65 to strengthen Australia's reply after a promising opening stand between Renshaw and Travis Head.
The pair added runs comfortably before off-spinner Simon Harmer struck twice in the same over. Head was bowled for 41 after chopping the ball onto his stumps, while Marnus Labuschagne fell for a five-ball duck after edging to slip.
Renshaw and Green then combined for a 126-run third-wicket partnership, taking Australia to 148/2 before lunch and continuing their stand into the afternoon session. Both batters brought up their half-centuries, with Green particularly aggressive against Kagiso Rabada.
However, Marco Jansen swung the momentum back South Africa's way by dismissing both set batters within two overs. Renshaw was caught behind after attempting to attack a short delivery, with the decision confirmed by DRS. The wicket was Jansen's 100th in Test cricket. Green followed soon after, edging to slip.
South Africa appeared to have regained control heading into the final session, but Inglis and Carey ensured Australia finished the day firmly on top.
The three-match series is level at 1-1. Australia won the opening Test in Durban by 214 runs, while South Africa bounced back with an innings-and-31-run victory in Gqeberha. The third and final Test in Cape Town remains finely poised, with Australia holding the advantage after a strong batting display.

stories.headline: Big setback for New Zealand! Star player ruled out of India T20I series
stories.deck: Lockie Ferguson, New Zealand's fast bowler, is out of the ongoing T20I series against India due to a calf injury. With India already leading 3-0, the team has summoned Matt Fisher to enhance their bowling strength. Concurrently, Matt Henry is on the mend from a quadricep injury but is expected to rejoin for the upcoming ODI clashes.
stories.bodyText:
New Zealand have suffered another injury setback ahead of the fourth T20I against India, with fast bowler Lockie Ferguson ruled out of the remainder of the series and Matt Fisher called up as his replacement.
Ferguson sustained an injury to his right calf during the second T20I at Hagley Oval. Scans subsequently confirmed a low-grade tear, with the pacer expected to need around another week of recovery before returning to action, New Zealand Cricket said in a statement on Thursday.
The latest blow comes at a time when New Zealand's fast-bowling attack has struggled to contain India's aggressive batting throughout the series. India have already secured an unassailable 3-0 lead, with their batters making light work of the hosts' bowling in all three matches.
India chased down 225 in the opening T20I before successfully pursuing a target of 180 in the second match. The third T20I proved even more punishing for New Zealand, as India overhauled 199 in just 13.2 overs.
While the pace attack has come under pressure, New Zealand's spinners Mitchell Santner and Michael Bracewell have continued to do a good job in the series.
Matt Henry on track for ODI series
New Zealand have also provided an update on Matt Henry, who experienced pain in his right quadricep during the second T20I. Subsequent assessment revealed a low-grade tear, with the fast bowler expected to require one to two weeks to recover.
Henry had been scheduled to return for the upcoming ODI series as part of a planned workload management programme. Despite the injury, he remains on track for that return.
Meanwhile, Kyle Jamieson will stay in Wellington under his planned workload management schedule. He is available to play for Canterbury in their second-round Ford Trophy match on Saturday before rejoining the national team on Monday ahead of the ODI series.
With the T20I series already decided, New Zealand will look to finish on a stronger note when the fourth match takes place at Eden Park in Auckland on Friday. The match is sold out, with India aiming to extend their dominance and the hosts seeking a response after three difficult outings with the ball.

stories.headline: Ranji Trophy: Andre guides Tamil Nadu home in a tense chase
stories.deck: The vice-captain makes the most of an early reprieve as the host overhauls the 128-run target by five wickets to register its second successive win; spinners Toufik and Raj bowl their heart out for Railways
stories.bodyText:
On a ragged MAC Stadium pitch, the Tamil Nadu batters successfully chased down 128, but not without a few nervy moments.
Day three started with Tamil Nadu getting the last Railways wicket for the addition of just one more run. And it ended with the home side doing just enough to win the Ranji Trophy Elite Group D fixture by five wickets.
Toufik Mondal (23.1-3-50-4) and Raj Choudhary (25-8-46-1) operated with control and precision, ensuring Tamil Nadu did not get any easy runs.
The host opted for a new opening pair on Wednesday, with S.R. Athish (coming off a blob in the previous innings) replacing Vimal Khumar (following back-to-back ducks) as N. Jagadeesan’s partner.
Just as Tamil Nadu was looking comfortable at 31 for no loss, three batters went back to the dugout playing rash shots coming down the track.
Jagadeesan was bowled playing all around one. Athish and No. 3 Sonu Yadav fell to catches in the deep — the former inexplicably going for a big hit immediately after striking Raj for a four.
B. Indrajith (23, 85b, 1x4) and Andre Siddarth (56 n.o., 128b, 2x4) then had a 50-run stand after the latter was dropped by skipper Bhargav Merai at mid-off with the total on 51.
Andre, though he stayed till the end to win the game for Tamil Nadu, was scratchy at best in the beginning.
The host again lost two wickets in a jiffy, with Indrajith getting caught behind and Pradosh Ranjan Paul struck in front after a futile attempt at a reverse sweep.
At 91 for five, Tamil Nadu was still not out of the woods. However, Andre and Vimal Khumar weathered the storm and sealed six points, making it two wins in a row for Sai Kishore & Co.

stories.headline: Terrific Threesome — redefining the slam-bang manual
stories.deck: India are blessed to have four equally aggressive and proven options to pick from to open the batting should it come to that. Abhishek, Samson, Sooryavanshi and Kishan are each more than a handful on his own; throw three, or even all four (like at the Asian Games) in the mix, and you can’t help but feel for the already beleaguered bowling community
stories.bodyText:
If cricket is a game of glorious uncertainties, then its 20-over variant is even more so. It’s no secret that the shorter the format, the more of a level-playing field it is, which is why ‘upsets’ are more commonplace in T20 cricket than in 50-over games or matches of longer durations.
One of the almost iron-clad certainties, even in the slam-bang version, is that if Abhishek Sharma plays a minimum of 10 deliveries, at least one six, if not more, is guaranteed. So complete is his command over his craft that he has established himself as the most valuable property in this format, wreaking such unimaginable havoc that oftentimes, opposition bowlers desperately wish for the earth to open up and gobble them up.
Tuesday at Wellington’s Hnry Stadium is the latest instance of the left-hander from Punjab snatching the game away from the opposition in the small matter of a half-hour. Trailing 0-2 in the five-match and perhaps aware that they had left at least 25 runs back in the changing room, New Zealand targeted early success to keep themselves in the hunt after posting 198. As it turned out, with no little help from the precocious, precious Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Abhishek made it decidedly a no-contest, raining fours and sixes with such stunning regularity that Mitchell Santner and his charges had nowhere to hide.
The vicissitudes of sport
No one has experienced the vicissitudes of sport, and specifically the T20 game, more than Abhishek — perhaps with the exception of his regular opening partner, Sanju Samson. He began 2026 in a blaze of glory with two half-centuries against the Kiwis at home, but each of those was succeeded by a first-ball blob. Then came the cruellest of cuts as India began their hunt to defend the T20 World Cup crown worn in Bridgetown in June 2024.
Abhishek was expected to set the tone for India’s dominance, but he made the most wretched of starts to his World Cup career. In the opener against United States in Mumbai, he was dismissed off the first ball of the contest, caught at deep cover. It was an unfortunate dismissal in the sense that he picked out the admittedly strategically placed fielder with unerring accuracy as he opened his shoulders and creamed a full, wide ball from paceman Ali Khan, looking to make his trademark opening statement with a signature six.
It happens, we all said, especially given the willingness with which Abhishek embraces risk. But it happened again, in his next match against Pakistan in Colombo (he missed the game against Namibia in Delhi after being hospitalised with a stomach infection). And in the fixture that followed, against Netherlands in Ahmedabad. Three ducks on the bounce, the last two also in the first over against off-spinners Salman Agha and Aryan Dutt respectively, suggested a pattern which compelled India to split their all-left opening combination of Abhishek and Ishan Kishan by bringing Samson into the equation.
Abhishek salvaged a most modest tournament with an authoritative half-century in the final against New Zealand, feeding off the show of confidence from the think-tank which didn’t so much as contemplate leaving him out despite 0, 0, 0 and 15 in his first four hits. His stunning early assault, with the by-now flowing Samson, sparked a first-wicket stand of 98 in a mere 43 deliveries, the foundation from which India closed out a commanding 96-run victory to retain their title in grand style in front of nearly 100,000 unashamedly partisan spectators at the Narendra Modi Stadium.
Thriving off his heroics in the final, Abhishek slipped back into his usual destructive mode thereafter, one of the few bright spots when India lost 0-6 to Ireland and England combined in June-July. A trough in Zimbabwe – 11 runs in three innings – was no more than a temporary blip. Upon return home, he smashed 108 off 34 balls against Afghanistan in Delhi, 61 (28b) in the Asian Games final against Pakistan in Nisshin and 69 (30b) against West Indies in Indore.
Frenzied starts
In New Zealand, he had got the team off to much-needed frenzied starts in the first two games, with 29 off 12 and 27 off 21 in stiff run-chases. Which brought us to the Hnry Stadium, where India were confronted with a target of 199 to take an unbeatable 3-0 lead.
For much of Abhishek’s post-World Cup run, his partner in crime was Samson. On and off, the latter made way to accommodate Sooryavanshi, most notably in Zimbabwe where the wicketkeeper from Keralam didn’t even figure in the extended squad after a run of modest scores following his Player-of-the-Tournament heroics in the World Cup.
For long, Samson has been one of the great enigmas of Indian cricket. When he is on song, he bats like a dream, making that vocation look ridiculously easy and straightforward. But then, he also lapses into frustrating inconsistency, which is what opened the door in the first place for Kishan’s reintegration with international cricket. Overlooked for the early part of the World Cup (except in Delhi in Abhishek’s unavailability), Samson was brought back in Chennai to offer a right-handed point of difference at the top of the tree, and responded with successive scores of 24, 97 not out, 89 and 89 (the last three in the knockouts) to become the toast of the nation.
Typically Samson-like, he followed that up with 5, 0 and 1 to make way for Sooryavanshi midway through the England series; chastened, he reeled off 57 and 50 in consecutive knocks against Afghanistan, then embarked on a string of 9, 7, 2 and 11 to ensure that he reprised a pattern that has been his constant companion all his career.
Why then would he not make half-centuries in three of his next five knocks? He wouldn’t be Samson otherwise, would he?
Abhishek’s mostly-off, now-on travails and Samson’s blow-hot blow-cold figures could paint the picture of the lack of substantial starts and early pressure on the incoming No. 3, mostly Kishan, and while there might be some truth to how that picture takes shape, the reality is also starkly surprising. The 26-year-old stylist from Amritsar and the 31-year-old purist from Thiruvananthapuram have been involved in five stands in excess of 50 in the 25 innings in which they have opened together this calendar year, equalling an Indian record held hitherto by K.L. Rahul and Rohit Sharma (in 2021) and by Abhishek himself and his good mate Shubman Gill (in 2025) when the latter made a brief if largely unsuccessful return to 20-over internationals.
Two to tango
Abhishek and Samson complement each other superbly; there is no competition, healthy or otherwise, no subconscious duel of one-upmanship, no trying to outdo each other. Both are comfortable in their respective skins, instinctively holding back when they sense that their partner is firing on all cylinders, and quickly taking over the lead role if the other is a little off-key. It helps that one is a left-hander and the other bats right-handed, because it then becomes practically impossible for the bowling group to line a particular type of batter up.
They target different areas of the ground – Abhishek’s on-side play has come on by leaps and bounds and his pick-up shot is a joy to behold even if it can sometimes be his kryptonite too – and hit different strokes to balls of the same length, driving the opposition ragged with their dominance, their chutzpah and their fearlessness, for which loads of credit must also be placed at the doorstep of successive leadership groups.
On Tuesday, Samson was pushed down to No. 3 so that Sooryavanshi, the boy wonder, could return to his preferred opening slot. In Christchurch on Saturday when Kishan was unavailable with an adductor injury, the lad from Bihar had batted at No. 3 and evidently struggled, piecing together an unconvincing four off eight deliveries. That was understandable, considering it was his first competitive outing for three weeks, since the Asian Games final on October 3.
Orchestrating the swap
Quickly realising that Samson’s greater experience could allow them to split up the successful opening combination by slotting him at one-drop and thrusting Sooryavanshi to his comfort zone, Shreyas Iyer and Gautam Gambhir orchestrated the swap that resulted in the highest ever PowerPlay score (118) in T20I history.
Sooryavanshi hammered four fours and as many sixes in a 19-ball 45, almost holding his own as his senior partner, Abhishek, tore into the bowling. That being said, it was Sooryavanshi who fired the first shots across the bows, hammering the first ball of the chase, from Jacob Duffy, over mid-on for four and clattering the third legal delivery of the innings over and behind point for a towering six. New Zealand ran into a revolving door; they were battered for 50 in just 2.2 overs, the fastest team fifty in all T20Is.
Abhishek brought up his half-century in 15 deliveries, and took another 20 balls for his second fifty. His 11th century meant he left the great Virat Kohli behind and became the Indian with the most 20-over hundreds; it was also his fourth T20I ton, a monumental accomplishment considering he has played just 69 innings.
Just to put things in perspective, Rohit Sharma (who holds the record for the most T20I hundreds alongside Glenn Maxwell), finished with five centuries from 151 hits, while Suryakumar Yadav, with whom Abhishek drew abreast, batted 107 times though that is offset by the fact that he didn’t always occupy the top three slots. In all T20s, only Chris Gayle (22) and Babar Azam (13) have more three-figure knocks than the rangy left-hander. With time, opportunity and ambition on his side, Abhishek won’t be playing second fiddle to many of these worthies for a long time.
India are blessed to have four equally aggressive and proven options to pick from to open the batting should it come to that. Abhishek, Samson, Sooryavanshi and Kishan are each more than a handful on his own; throw three, or even all four (like at the Asian Games) in the mix, and you can’t help but feel for the already beleaguered bowling community. As a popular catchline for a television brand goes: Neighbour’s Envy, Owner’s Pride.

briefs.headline: ‘Threatened and discriminated’: Sangakkara alleges discrimination by staff in Dublin
briefs.deck: Kumar Sangakkara recently recounted a distressing experience involving alleged discrimination by Ryanair staff at Dublin airport. He found the encounter shocking and used social media to connect with others who faced similar situations. This incident has sparked a significant dialogue about the issues of anti-Asian racism and xenophobia in Ireland, while Ryanair remains silent regarding these…
briefs.bodyText:
Former Sri Lanka captain 
Kumar Sangakkara
 has alleged that Ryanair staff threatened and discriminated against his family at an airport in Dublin, with his account triggering a discussion on social media.
Kumar Sangakkara post
The 
Rajasthan Royals
 head coach took to X on Wednesday evening to share his experience, describing the encounter with the airline's gate personnel as shocking. He also called it his first unpleasant experience in Dublin, the capital of Ireland.
“Has anyone experienced discriminatory gate personnel @Ryanair in Dublin? I, with my family, just did and it was shocking," Sangakkara tweeted on Wednesday evening.
Sangakkara's post drew reactions from social media users, including fellow Sri Lankan Sanjiva Weerawarana, who spoke about his own experiences of discrimination while living and travelling overseas.
“Kumar, I have experienced discrimination in every part of the West. I lived there for 16 years, travelled back and forth for another 25 and now I’m done," the individual replied.
Responding to Weerawarana, Sangakkara acknowledged the distress such encounters can cause.
“It’s quite jarring when you experience it," Sangakkara said.
The exchange added to the discussion surrounding the former Sri Lankan skipper's allegations and the treatment of passengers by airline personnel. 
At the time of writing, Ryanair had not issued a response to Sangakkara's claims.
Ryanair is an Irish ultra-low-cost airline headquartered in Swords, County Dublin. The incident has also brought attention to concerns about anti-Asian racism and xenophobia in Ireland, which can range from everyday prejudice and online abuse to physical assaults.
Sangakkara's coaching career and international record
Sangakkara, regarded as one of Sri Lanka's greatest cricketers, retired from international cricket in 2015 after a distinguished career across formats.
As Rajasthan Royals coach, Sangakkara ended the franchise’s 17-year wait to reach another final during his first tenure. However, the Royals finished runners-up to Gujarat Titans. In 2026, Rajasthan bowed out in Qualifier 2, falling one win short of the final.
Sangakkara's Test career began against South Africa in Galle on July 20, 2000, and concluded in Colombo after 134 matches. He accumulated 12,400 runs, including 38 centuries and 52 half-centuries. He finished one short of Australian great Donald Bradman's record of 12 double centuries.
In ODIs, Sangakkara played 404 matches after making his debut in 2000, scoring 14,234 runs at an average of almost 42. His highest score was 169, while his tally included 25 centuries and 93 half-centuries.
He brought his 50-over international career to an end after the 2015 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand. Sangakkara was part of Sri Lanka teams that finished runners-up at the 2007 and 2011 editions of the tournament.

briefs.headline: ‘Vaibhav heads out’: Ashwin’s blunt call on Sooryavanshi if Ishan Kishan returns
briefs.deck: Ravichandran Ashwin has urged fans and experts to be patient with young player Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. He believes Sooryavanshi showcased his talent in the latest T20I match, contributing to India's successful chase. Meanwhile, Ashwin has suggested that Sanju Samson should reclaim his opening position if Ishan Kishan re-enters the lineup. Ashwin expressed concern over the expectations placed on…
briefs.bodyText:
Former India spinner 
Ravichandran Ashwin
 has called for patience with teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, urging fans and experts not to burden the youngster with expectations too early in his career. 
Ashwin
 also believes Sooryavanshi should make way for 
Sanju Samson
 at the top of the order if Ishan Kishan returns to the playing XI for the next T20I against New Zealand.
Sooryavanshi made an immediate impact in the third T20I, hammering 45 off just 19 deliveries as India chased down a target of 199 with 6.4 overs to spare. The teenager shared a record-breaking 133-run opening stand with Abhishek Sharma, underlining his ability to take on the opposition from the outset.
Praising the youngster's fearless approach, Ashwin said Sooryavanshi had already shown glimpses of his exceptional talent throughout the IPL and predicted a bright future for him.
"The way Vaibhav Sooryavanshi just took off was something that he has done all IPL. For me, he is and will always be a very special player. I look forward to seeing him do very many special things in his career," Ashwin said on SonyLiv.
However, Ashwin feels Samson should reclaim his opening position if Kishan is available for the next match. With Kishan's injury having opened the door for Sooryavanshi, Samson had moved to No. 3 in the previous game. 
The veteran spinner believes Samson's experience makes him capable of adapting to the role, but his performances have earned him the right to open.
"In this combination, when Ishan Kishan is missing and Sooryavanshi has to come, that probably looks like the perfect order because Sanju has got the experience to be able to deal with going in at No. 3. However, tomorrow if Ishan Kishan is going to come back, I think Vaibhav heads out and Sanju slots right back into the slot he deserves," he added.
Ashwin urges patience with Sooryavanshi
Beyond the selection debate, Ashwin's bigger concern is ensuring that the 15-year-old gets enough room to develop without the weight of expectations. While acknowledging that Sooryavanshi could become one of Indian cricket's biggest names in the future, he stressed that the youngster should be allowed to enjoy the game.
"These are all big statements to make so early in his life. I really hope that the young boy gets that breathing space. I know he is going to be the poster boy of Indian cricket at some stage, but we all need to take that backward step and allow him to enjoy his cricket," said Ashwin.
Drawing from his own early years in the game, Ashwin explained why it was important not to rush to conclusions about a young player's future based on a few standout performances.
"I have played cricket from a very young age, and at 16, I was enjoying cricket in the maidans in some club grounds in Chennai. That's what a 16-year-old is supposed to do. He did something spectacular today (Tuesday). I won't jump to any conclusions. He is a talent to watch out for. Let him enjoy his cricket, and let's also enjoy watching him bat," he explained.
Sooryavanshi was drafted into the playing XI for the second T20I after Kishan picked up an injury, but struggled to make an impact at No. 3, scoring just four runs off eight balls.
For the third T20I, Samson made way for the teenager at the top of the order, allowing him to partner Abhishek. The move paid off as the duo produced a record-breaking opening partnership to put India firmly on course for the chase.
With Kishan potentially returning for the next game, the team management could face a decision over the batting order, with Ashwin backing Samson to resume his place as opener and Sooryavanshi to continue his development away from the immediate spotlight.

briefs.headline: WPL auction: Molineux, Kiran top earners; Kashvi scripts history
briefs.deck: UP Warriorz drafts in the T20 WC-winning captain for ₹1.10 crore; the Indian big-hitter to turn out for Capitals after being bought for ₹75 lakh; the 15-year-old is the youngest to make a WPL squad
briefs.bodyText:
Just a cricket ball’s throw away from Hyatt Grand lies the peaceful Vembanad Lake. The WPL’s mini auction, held at Hyatt’s Vembanad Hall, was about just as peaceful on Wednesday evening: there weren’t that many fierce bidding wars.
That wasn’t really surprising. It was a mini auction, after all, with just 27 slots up for grabs. Sophie Molineux, the all-rounder who led Australia to the T20 World Cup crown some three months ago in England, turned out to be the costliest star. She was bought by UP Warriorz for ₹1.10 crore.
Warriorz had come to the auction with by far the largest purse (₹3.75 crore), and the paddle from their table went up even before the auctioneer completed announcing Molineux’s name. Her base price was ₹50 lakh. Royal Challengers Bengaluru was also keen, but had to step back as it didn’t have the kind of money that Warriorz had.
Warriorz, of course, had more spots to fill than the other four franchises. They went on to add Grace Harris (₹30 lakh), Sneh Rana (₹30 lakh), Sushma Verma (₹30 lakh), Asha Sobhana (₹30 lakh), Kathryn Bryce (₹10 lakh), Manali Dakshini (₹10 lakh) and Sahana Pawar (₹10 lakh).
Among them, the biggest steal was Harris, one of the hardest hitters you would come across in women’s cricket. She can be more than useful with her off-spin, too. She is returning to Warriorz after being part of the title-winning RCB.
Another big-hitter, Kiran Navgire, did not come as cheap: Delhi Capitals bought her for ₹75 lakh, against a base price of ₹40 lakh. Mumbai Indians was also interested in her.
G. Kamalini and Jess Jonassen were both picked up for their base price of ₹40 lakh, by Gujarat Giants and RCB, respectively. Mumbai Indians went on a spree of budget buys. It got Disha Kasat, Latika Inamdar, Bharti Rawal, Saanika Chalke and Akshita Bhagat, all for ₹10 lakh, and Shweta Sehrawat for ₹20 lakh.
Uma Kashvi was sold for ₹10 lakh to Capitals, but she made history. At 15, she is the youngest to make it to a WPL squad.
There were big stars who failed to shine, like Sophia Dunkley. The England opener was the only player, apart from Molineux, who had asked for a base price of ₹50 lakh. She had no takers.

briefs.headline: World Wrestling C'ships: India script history as Neelam, Kajal settle for silver
briefs.deck: India’s Kajal Dhochak and Neelam Sirohi created history by winning silver medals at the World Wrestling Championships in Astana, becoming the first Indian women to reach finals at the same edition. Kajal narrowly lost 6-8 to Ukraine’s Anastasiya Alpyeyeva, while Neelam fell to Japan’s Yui Susaki, securing India’s landmark double-silver finish.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: With 30 seconds left and the scores locked at 4-4, Kajal Dhochak stood on the brink of a golden finish. The 18-year-old Indian had fought her way back into contention, but just when victory appeared within reach, Ukraine’s Anastasiya Alpyeyeva struck decisively. Kajal’s spirited resistance ended in an agonising 6-8 defeat in the women’s 76kg final at the World Wrestling Championships in Astana on Wednesday.
The heartbreak, however, could not overshadow a landmark day for Indian wrestling. Kajal and Neelam Sirohi claimed silver medals, becoming the first Indian women to reach the finals of the same edition of the senior Worlds.
Kajal, competing at the senior Worlds for the first time, began the final on the back foot, trailing 1-3 after the opening three-minute period. She regrouped impressively in the second half, clawing her way back to level the contest at 4-4.
With the bout finely poised, Alpyeyeva, a two-time European champion, executed a crucial move and exposure angle to establish an 8-4 advantage. Kajal managed a late takedown, but the deficit proved insurmountable.
The silver capped an impressive campaign for the teenager, a two-time under-20 world champion, who had produced a stunning 10-7 comeback victory over Kyrgyzstan’s Aiperi Medet Kyzy after trailing 1-7 in the semifinals.
Earlier, Neelam faced arguably the toughest examination of her career against Japan’s Yui Susaki, one of freestyle wrestling’s most accomplished champions, in the women’s 50kg final.
The 26-year-old Indian, who had defeated Kazakhstan’s Zeinep Bayanova 7-3 to reach the title clash, encountered an opponent operating at an extraordinary level. Susaki established a 5-0 lead before pinning Neelam towards the end of the opening period, sealing another world title without conceding a point throughout her tournament campaign.
The victory secured Susaki’s fifth World Championships crown. The Japanese star had previously won gold once in the 48kg category and three times at 50kg, underlining her sustained dominance.
For Neelam, the silver was a significant breakthrough after missing out on an Asian Games selection spot earlier this year.
Until now, Anshu Malik’s silver in the 57kg category at the 2021 Worlds in Oslo had stood alone as an Indian woman’s runner-up finish at the senior championships.
Neelam and Kajal have now changed that narrative, delivering an impressive double-silver finish to strengthen the nation's growing presence in women’s wrestling.

briefs.headline: Molineux mania! UP Warriorz outgun RCB in Rs 1.10 cr showstopper at WPL auction
briefs.deck: UP Warriorz secured Australia captain Sophie Molineux for Rs 1.10 crore after a bidding battle with RCB at the WPL mini auction in Kochi. They also signed Grace Harris, Sushma Verma and Sneh Rana, prioritising experience. Delhi Capitals bought Kiran Navgire for ₹75 lakh, while Gujarat Giants signed Gunalan Kamalini. Sri Lankan veteran Chamari Athapaththu surprisingly went unsold.
briefs.bodyText:
KOCHI: UP Warriorz, with the biggest purse of Rs 3.75 crore, beat Royal Challengers Bengaluru in a fierce bidding war to sign Australia captain 
Sophie Molineux
 for Rs 1.10 crore at the WPL mini auction in Kochi on Wednesday.
UP opened at Rs 50 lakh and RCB, for whom Molineux was part of the 2024 title-winning side, came straight back, and her price zoomed to Rs 95 lakh. UP then moved it to Rs 1 crore, the RCB countered at Rs 1.05 crore. UP finally pushed it to Rs 1.10 crore to seal the deal. Allrounder Molineux is the X-factor, who provides a wealth of experience for UP, and will be propped up as the perfect foil to her captain and compatriot, Meg Lanning.
“We were determined to get Sophie at any cost,” UP Warriorz CEO Kshemal Waingankar told reporters. “It puts us in a good position with Sophie and Grace (Harris) combined to tweak our combinations and decide what works best for us.”
UP added firepower to their batting by picking Australian 
Grace Harris
 for Rs 30 lakh, who returns to the franchise she represented in 2025. She had a prolific run in RCB’s 2026 title season, but was released with Ellyse Perry’s return. 
Harris is likely to open with Lanning or Pratika Rawal. With Harleen Deol also in the mix, it gives UP the legroom to mix and match their batters. “Grace brings power to the middle order, Molineux the leadership qualities,” Waingankar added.
They also snapped up experienced Himachal wicketkeeper Sushma Verma and bid Rs 30 lakh for offspinner Sneh Rana. With Sophie Ecclestone and Deepti Sharma in the squad, their spin attack looks robust.
Unlike previous seasons, UP went into this auction with a clear plan. “We carried out some experiments last season that didn’t work. This season, we were betting on experience, which is why we targeted players like Sushma Verma,” UP head coach Abhishek Nayar said.
Combinations were the priority for the five franchises, and with the other four on limited purse, the bidding remained largely cautious.
Gunalan Kamalini, the young India batter with a high ceiling went to Gujarat Giants who made the first bid at Rs 40 lakh. RCB opened their account by snapping up Australian left-arm spinner Jess Jonassen at a base price of Rs 40 lakh.
Mumbai Indians (MI) pursued Kiran Navigare, a former UP player, for a base price of Rs 40 lakh. Delhi Capitals took the price to Rs 75 lakh, and MI, with only Rs 90 lakh left in their purse, dropped out.
Sri Lankan veteran Chamari Athapaththu going unsold was the biggest surprise of the evening. MI played it smart by picking childhood friends Disha Kasat and Latika Imandar, two players from Vidarbha who have been making waves at the domestic level, for Rs 10 lakh each.
The auction’s biggest takeaway was the continuing importance of domestic cricket to women’s game, with franchises backing a raft of players who have emerged from the circuit.
Steal buys
Grace Harris (Rs 30 lakh, UP): Apart from her blistering strokeplay, she can bowl offspin in the Powerplay.
Sushma Verma (Rs 30 lakh, UP): An international player currently in stellar form. Got exposure in the CPL. She walks into UP’s playing XI given her keeping skills and experience.
Disha Kasat (Rs 10 lakh, MI): An improved player from WPL 2023. She can be used as an opener.
Kathryn Bryce (Rs 10 lakh, UP): Scotland captain, who can bowl medium pace and bat at the top of the order.
Sanika Chalke (Rs 10 lakh, MI): Touted as the player of the future. Part of the 2025 U-19 T20 World Cup-winning squad.
Samaira Raghav (Rs 10 lakh, GG): A16-year-old ex-sprinter who was pushed to cricket by her father. Currently making waves in Women’s DPL.
Top picks
Asha endures steep pay cut
UP Warriorz released Keralam leg spinner Asha Shobana for Rs 1.2 crore, then bagged her for a base price of Rs 30 lakh.
Orla Prendergast became the first Irish cricketer to be picked in the WPL. The Gujarat Giants roped the allrounder for Rs 30 lakh.

briefs.headline: World under-19 champ Aditya targets LA Olympics
briefs.bodyText:
For someone who switched from orthodox to southpaw stance, 17-year-old Aditya Singh owes his 55kg title win at the World Boxing under-19 championships in Montenegro to the hard yards he put in during his training.
Hailing from Bharan village of Rohtak district in Haryana, Aditya reached his coach Vinod Kumar, a former National bronze medallist in 2006, in Meham six years ago with a modest target of getting into the Army Boys Sports Company – a pathway to employment. But, Vinod saw some spark in the kid.
“For the first six months, nothing worked. He was an orthodox boxer, but his father never told me that. I decided to give another six months and see his performance as a southpaw. It produced results,” Vinod, also the basics coach of Olympian Preeti Pawar at Meham Boxing Club, told The Hindu.
Apart from Vinod, Aditya, a former National junior champion and an Asian under-19 silver medallist, is grateful to his farmer father Mahender Singh, who took his son to Meham, about 20km from their village, daily for training.
The teenager, who landed in the colder Montenegro two days prior to his first fight, outsmarted USA’s Futures Cup champion Christian Paez with a RSC verdict in the second round.
“I adapted after my first fight,” Aditya, who idolises Vassily Lomachenko and Andy Cruz, told The Hindu.
He counted his gains from his five wins against boxers from three continents. “The opponents, including two southpaws, had different techniques. I learnt a lot,” said Aditya, who also got past Serbia’s Filip Stanojevic 5-0, Italy’s Tommaso Orlando 5-0, Azerbaijan’s Nihat Gasimov 5-0 and Russian Islam Magomedov 4-1 to claim India’s lone gold medal.
Coach Ramanand of the Indian team praised Aditya for his hard work and adaptability. “Aditya was good in listening to the coaches and adapting well as per the situation. In the final against the Russian, he rallied from 2-3 in the first round to win the bout,” said Ramanand.
While Aditya looks to continue as an age-group boxer, Vinod targets Los Angeles 2028. “He deserves to be in the next Olympics. He stands out with his dedication and discipline,” said Vinod.

briefs.headline: Vijay hopes to show that off-spinners can excel in both Tests and T20s
briefs.deck: The Andhra tweaker sheds light on his transition from playing on cement tracks to turf wickets; the 25-year-old has been making rapid strides
briefs.bodyText:
T. Vijay is a lanky off-spinner with an uncomplicated action.
He gets the ball to drift and dip without losing accuracy for long. Combined with the turn on offer, these qualities make him a tricky bowler to face.
For much of his cricketing journey, however, Vijay had little idea about the finer aspects of the game. Hailing from Tekkali in Andhra Pradesh’s Srikakulam district, he started playing cricket on the only cement pitch his town had.
“There is only one net and one cement wicket. There is nothing beyond that. I had no idea about turf wickets,” Vijay told The Hindu.
It was only after joining an academy in Vizianagaram that he encountered a turf wicket and gradually learnt more about the sport. “I learnt about strength training, fitness, running and everything else. Before that, I only knew how to bowl. I didn’t know much about other aspects of cricket or how professional cricket worked,” the 25-year-old said.
With the support of his coaches Vikram Verma and C.D. Thomson, whom he met in Vizianagaram, and his family, Vijay began his journey.
In four years of senior cricket, Vijay has played 19 First Class matches and taken 65 wickets. He has also featured in 14 List A matches and 11 T20s — performances that have drawn the attention of selectors and scouts.
He made his IPL debut in 2026 with Delhi Capitals, after which he featured in South Zone’s squad in the Duleep Trophy.
Subsequently, he received his maiden India-A call-up as well for the two multi-day matches against Australia-A.
Vijay is aware that traditional off-spin is a dying art in modern cricket and that’s exactly what pushes him forward.
“It motivates me to come out of my comfort zone. I want to show everyone that off-spinners can also do well in T20s and Test cricket. That’s my motto, and I will keep working hard and hope to do wonders,” Vijay concluded.
Day three washed out
Persistent rain overnight following Cyclone Arnab’s landfall brought an end to day three of the Ranji Trophy Group ‘B’ clash between Andhra and Chhattisgarh without any play here at the DVR Ground on Wednesday.
Both sides will hope conditions improve on the final day, with three points still in sight. Chhattisgarh is 15 runs behind Andhra’s first-innings total of 231 but has lost eight wickets. Amandeep Khare is unbeaten on 74 while Vijay has picked three wickets so far.

briefs.headline: Vaishnavi’s five-for sets up India’s series sweep
briefs.bodyText:
Zimbabwe’s historic maiden tour of India ended on a sobering note for the Lady Chevrons, with Vaishnavi Sharma’s maiden five-wicket haul and fifties from Pratika Rawal and Shafali Verma guiding India to a dominant eight-wicket win and a 3-0 series sweep here on Wednesday.
People in Vadodara are simple. They like their food and cricket. They particularly like their local stars being involved in international fixtures. At the BCA Stadium, from the security personnel to the ground staff, Yastika Bhatia was the name on everyone’s lips. After frustrating the home fans twice, India finally swapped out Richa Ghosh for her.
Yastika had a great afternoon behind the stumps, taking a catch and effecting a stumping and a run out, in an effort that restricted Zimbabwe to just 131 in 39.5 overs. But she botched a perfect opportunity to make a statement with the bat, going grand off the very first ball of the innings, only to find Francisca Chipare at mid-on.
Harleen Deol, in for Tejal Hasabnis, was overshadowed by Pratika’s fluency and fell for a run-a-ball 19. Pratika and Shafali, visibly in a hurry, got the job done at T20 pace with 33 overs to spare.
Earlier, Sayali Satghare and Kranti Gaud nipped Zimbabwe’s dream of a competitive score in the bud, leaving it stuttering at 12 for two by the third over. Inexperience showed as the visitors struggled to rotate strike and crumbled under dot ball pressure — a staggering 193 in 237 balls.
Modester Mupachikwa resisted, but Vaishnavi’s left-arm spin gobbled up the middle-order. The Gwalior-born bowler also registered India’s first no ball of the series and had a few going wide with the turn which she got on a slow track in Kotambi. But, a maiden ODI five-for brightened the day and she eventually led India off the field with a wide smile and her signature curtain call.
The scores: Zimbabwe 131 in 39.5 overs (Modester Mupachikwa 37, Josephine Nkomo 35, Vaishnavi Sharma 5/39) lost to India 133/2 in 17 overs (Pratika Rawal 59 n.o., Shafali Verma 51 n.o.). Toss: Zimbabwe; PoM: Vaishnavi; PoS: Pratika.
